explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The Teacher doesn't pick and choose here. He says, "Futility of futilities! Everything is futile!" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). That word "Everything" leaves no corner of the bakery untouched, not even the good cookies. He is going big on purpose, and the rest of the passage shows him walking through his list.

Yes, friend. The Teacher says "Everything is futile!" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). He doesn't say some things or a few things. He says everything, and he says "futility of futilities" like a man who has thought about it for a while. It's a big opening line, and it sets up everything else he looks at.

explanations.answer: What a man gains from it
explanations.explanation: That's the question, friend. The Teacher asks, "What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?" (Ecclesiastes 1:3). He's looking at the pile of work and asking what comes out the other end. I've asked myself that after a long day at the ovens, usually while scraping dough off my hat.

explanations.answer: How long a man must keep at it
explanations.explanation: Close, but he isn't counting the hours. The Teacher asks, "What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?" (Ecclesiastes 1:3). His question is about the gain, what a man ends up with. Nobody asks him to clock in here, friend, he just wants to know what the work brings.

explanations.answer: Who a man is working for
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but the Teacher doesn't ask about a boss. He asks, "What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?" (Ecclesiastes 1:3). The question is about gain, not about who signs the paycheck. Even I'd like to know who I'm working for sometimes, and my answer is a very good one.

That's it, friend. The Teacher says, "Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever." (Ecclesiastes 1:4). People come and go, and the ground stays put. It's like the counter in a kitchen that has seen a hundred batches and doesn't even say thank you.

Good guess, but the Teacher says the opposite. He says, "Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever." (Ecclesiastes 1:4). The generations are the ones coming and going. The earth is the steady one in this line, and it stays right where it is.

Nice try, friend, but the earth isn't going anywhere in this verse. The Teacher says, "Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever." (Ecclesiastes 1:4). The people are the ones on the move, passing through one after another. The earth is the one thing that stays.

explanations.answer: Hurries back to where it rises
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. The Teacher says the sun "hurries back to where it rises." (Ecclesiastes 1:5). It sets, and then it's already rushing back to start again. No lunch break, no nap, just straight back to the beginning. I know that kind of schedule.

Not this time. The sun in this verse doesn't park itself anywhere. The Teacher says it rises and sets, and then it "hurries back to where it rises." (Ecclesiastes 1:5). It keeps on the move, friend, and it's in a hurry about it.

That sounds nice, but the verse has no rest in it. The Teacher says the sun rises and sets, and then it "hurries back to where it rises." (Ecclesiastes 1:5). Nobody calls it and it doesn't wait around. It goes straight back to the start, friend.

That's right, friend. The Teacher says the wind swirls "round and round," "ever returning on its course." (Ecclesiastes 1:6). South, then north, then around again. If I followed that wind, I'd end up right back at my own oven door.

Nope, this wind doesn't quit. The Teacher says it swirls "round and round," "ever returning on its course." (Ecclesiastes 1:6). It keeps coming back, and nothing in the verse says it ever stops, friend.

Good try, but the sea is in a different verse. About the wind, the Teacher says it swirls "round and round," "ever returning on its course." (Ecclesiastes 1:6). It doesn't leave, friend. It circles back and goes again.

True, friend. The Teacher says, "All the rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is never full" (Ecclesiastes 1:7). Every river keeps pouring in and the sea still has room. I wish my cookie boxes worked like that. Actually, I take that back, I'd never get to rest.

This one is true, friend. The Teacher says, "All the rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is never full" (Ecclesiastes 1:7). The rivers keep pouring in and the sea never fills up. It's a strange picture, and he chose it on purpose.

explanations.answer: Back to the place they came from
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The Teacher says, "to the place from which the streams come, there again they flow." (Ecclesiastes 1:7). The water goes right back to where it started, and then it all begins again. It's a circle, and the water is the one walking it.

Not quite. The verse has the water going somewhere, but not to stay. The Teacher says, "to the place from which the streams come, there again they flow." (Ecclesiastes 1:7). It heads back to where it came from, friend.

Good guess, but the wilderness isn't in this verse. The Teacher says, "to the place from which the streams come, there again they flow." (Ecclesiastes 1:7). The streams head back to where they started, and the loop begins over.

That's it, friend. The Teacher says, "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing." (Ecclesiastes 1:8). You can look and listen all day, and they still want more. That's a lot like me watching a tray of cookies come out and still wanting one more look.

explanations.answer: They lose their strength with age
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thing to think, but the verse doesn't say it. The Teacher says, "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing." (Ecclesiastes 1:8). He's talking about never being satisfied, not about getting older, friend.

explanations.answer: They catch only what is near
explanations.explanation: Close in spirit, but the verse isn't about distance. The Teacher says, "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing." (Ecclesiastes 1:8). The eye and ear just never get their fill, friend, however much they take in.

You got it, friend. The Teacher says, "there is nothing new under the sun." (Ecclesiastes 1:9). What has been will be again, and what has been done will be done again. Even my newest recipe feels like it has a cousin somewhere.

Good guess, but that's not the word. The Teacher says, "there is nothing new under the sun." (Ecclesiastes 1:9). He's saying what has been will be again, so nothing is brand new. Hidden is a fine word, it just isn't this verse.

Not this one, friend. The Teacher says, "there is nothing new under the sun." (Ecclesiastes 1:9). His point is that what has been will be again, so nothing counts as new. Certain is a good word, but he doesn't use it here.

Careful, friend, because it's the other way around. The Teacher says, "There is no remembrance of those who came before, and those yet to come will not be remembered by those who follow after." (Ecclesiastes 1:11). The people yet to come will not be remembered by the ones after them. That's a heavy line, and I'll say it plainly.

That's right, friend. The Teacher says, "those yet to come will not be remembered by those who follow after." (Ecclesiastes 1:11). He says no remembrance, not for those who came before and not for those yet to come. It's a heavy line, and he doesn't soften it.
